_README: THE JUDGE FOR LOOP B. Every `expected` value here must be TRANSCRIBED BY A HUMAN (or a model with a cited source) from published NASA/Espenak local-circumstances output or Jubier's interactive maps. A value the solver produced is NOT ground truth — it is the thing under test. gate_b.py REFUSES TO RUN while any anchor is unpopulated. This is structural: it makes fabricating ground truth impossible rather than merely forbidden.
_how_to_populate: 1. Open NASA/Espenak local circumstances (or Jubier's map) for the eclipse date.
2. Enter the observer lat/lon exactly as given below.
3. Transcribe: time of max eclipse (UT), sun altitude at max, duration of totality, in_umbra.
4. Record the URL you read it from in `source`.
Do NOT round. Do NOT infer. If a source doesn't give a value, leave it null and note why.

ancient._note: Position tolerance is NOT a fixed number. It is the delta-T uncertainty band from outputs/delta_t_decision.json for that era. Earth turns 15 deg/hour: a 1-hour delta-T error moves the path ~1500 km. Report the band; do not pretend to precision you do not have.

crosscheck_besselian_vs_skyfield._note: Two independent methods must agree with EACH OTHER, tighter than either agrees with published values.

anchors.why: THE CANARY. The human's actual observing site. Low-sun totality on Spain's east coast. If the engine gets this wrong, nothing else in the project is trustworthy — and unlike every other anchor, this one gets validated against reality in person.
Second point on the same path, well inland — catches a solver that gets one point right by luck.
NEGATIVE CONTROL. Outside the path of totality. A solver that says 'yes' to everything passes every positive test. This one must return in_umbra: false.
The most heavily documented eclipse in history. Ground truth is abundant and unambiguous. High sun altitude — the opposite regime from the Spain anchor.
The longest totality of the 21st century, and it falls on Jul 22 — the project's top-ranked date. Tests the long-duration end of the range.
Recent, extremely well documented, northern latitude. Tests the oblateness correction where it bites hardest.

anchors.eclipse_date: TBD — pick a well-studied ancient eclipse with historical records
anchors.why: DELTA-T STRESS TEST. Candidates: the 763 BCE Bur-Sagale eclipse (Assyrian record), or Thales' eclipse (585 BCE). These are the events historians used to CONSTRAIN delta-T in the first place. The point is not to nail the position — it is to confirm the engine's error stays inside the documented uncertainty band from B2. Passing this with suspiciously tight agreement is itself a red flag: it means delta-T is being applied twice, or not at all.
